title: Welcome: shapes, match and Result
source:
# Welcome to the Astra playground.
#
# Edit this program and press Run (Ctrl+Enter). It runs on Astra's
# interpreter, inside your browser: same output as a native build.
# Check shows the JSON an agent reads; Fix repairs what it can.

struct Size:
    w: int
    h: int

enum Shape:
    Square(int)
    Rect(Size)
    Triangle(Size)

fn area(s: Shape) -> int:
    match s:
        Shape::Square(side) => return side * side
        Shape::Rect(size) => return size.w * size.h
        Shape::Triangle(size) => return size.w * size.h / 2

fn largest(shapes: [Shape]) -> Result<int, str>:
    if shapes.length() == 0:
        return Result::Err("no shapes")
    let best = 0
    for s in shapes:
        let a = area(s)
        if a > best:
            best = a
    return Result::Ok(best)

fn main() -> int:
    let shapes = [Shape::Square(5), Shape::Rect(Size { w: 3, h: 4 }), Shape::Triangle(Size { w: 6, h: 9 })]
    for s in shapes:
        print("area ${area(s)}")
    match largest(shapes):
        Result::Ok(a) => print("largest: ${a}")
        Result::Err(why) => print("error: ${why}")
    return 0

# 06_arrays_and_loops.astra — lists and loops
#
# `for x in xs` walks a list, `for i in a..b` counts (b excluded), `while`
# repeats, `break` and `continue` work as usual. Every index is
# bounds-checked: reading past the end stops with a clear runtime error.

fn sum(xs: [int]) -> int:
    let total = 0
    for x in xs:
        total += x
    return total

fn main() -> int:
    let numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
    print("sum of ${numbers.length()} numbers = ${sum(numbers)}")

    numbers.push(60)
    numbers[0] = 5
    print("after push(60) and numbers[0] = 5: sum = ${sum(numbers)}")

    let squares = 0
    let i = 1
    while i <= 5:
        squares += i * i
        i += 1
    print("sum of squares 1..5 = ${squares}")

    let factorial = 1
    for j in 1..7:
        factorial *= j
    print("6! = ${factorial}")

    let found = -1
    for n in 0..100:
        if n % 7 != 0:
            continue
        if n > 40:
            found = n
            break
    print("first multiple of 7 above 40: ${found}")
    return 0

title: Errors are values: Result<T, E> and `?`
source:
# 07_error_handling.astra — errors are values: Result<T, E> and `?`
#
# A function that can fail says so in its type. The caller must handle both
# arms of the Result; `?` passes an error up instead. Built-ins that can
# fail (parse_int, read_file, ...) work the same way.

fn divide(a: int, b: int) -> Result<int, str>:
    if b == 0:
        return Result::Err("cannot divide ${a} by zero")
    return Result::Ok(a / b)

fn average(total: int, count: int) -> Result<int, str>:
    let mean = divide(total, count)?
    return Result::Ok(mean)

fn or_zero(r: Result<int, str>) -> int:
    match r:
        Result::Ok(v) => return v
        Result::Err(e) => return 0

fn main() -> int:
    match divide(10, 2):
        Result::Ok(v) => print("10 / 2 = ${v}")
        Result::Err(e) => print("error: ${e}")

    match divide(10, 0):
        Result::Ok(v) => print("10 / 0 = ${v}")
        Result::Err(e) => print("error: ${e}")

    match average(90, 0):
        Result::Ok(v) => print("average = ${v}")
        Result::Err(e) => print("average failed: ${e}")

    print("with a fallback: ${or_zero(divide(7, 0))}")
    assert_eq(or_zero(divide(9, 3)), 3)
    print("all Result checks passed")
    return 0

title: Structs built, passed and returned
source:
# 08_structs_mixed_fields.astra — structs built, passed and returned
#
# Fields keep their declared types (str, int, bool). Structs can be created
# in one function and returned to another, nested inside other structs, and
# kept in lists.

struct Person:
    name: str
    age: int
    email: str
    active: bool

struct Team:
    lead: Person
    name: str

fn new_person(name: str, age: int) -> Person:
    let email = name.to_lower() + "@example.com"
    return Person { name: name, age: age, email: email, active: true }

fn summary(p: Person) -> str:
    let status = p.active ? "active" : "inactive"
    return "${p.name} (${p.age}), ${p.email}, ${status}"

fn main() -> int:
    let alice = new_person("Alice", 30)
    print(summary(alice))
    assert_eq(alice.age, 30)

    let team = Team { lead: alice, name: "Compilers" }
    print("team ${team.name} is led by ${team.lead.name}")

    let people = [alice, new_person("Bob", 25), new_person("Chen", 41)]
    let total = 0
    for p in people:
        total += p.age
    print("${people.length()} people, combined age ${total}")
    return 0

title: Nominal traits and trait bounds
source:
# 09_traits.astra — nominal traits and trait bounds (A8)
#
# A `trait` declares method signatures; an `impl Trait for Type` block
# implements them. A generic function bounded by the trait (`fn f<T: Shape>`)
# can call the trait's methods, dispatched statically per concrete type.

trait Shape:
    fn area(self) -> int

struct Circle:
    r: int

struct Square:
    s: int

impl Shape for Circle:
    fn area(self) -> int:
        return self.r * self.r

impl Shape for Square:
    fn area(self) -> int:
        return self.s * self.s

fn total<T: Shape>(s: T) -> int:
    return s.area()

fn main() -> int:
    print("Circle area: " + total(Circle { r: 3 }).to_string())
    print("Square area: " + total(Square { s: 4 }).to_string())
    return 0

title: Structs and lists are values
source:
# 10_value_semantics.astra — structs and lists are values (A8)
#
# Assignment copies: changing `b` never changes `a`. A function changes its
# caller's value only through a `mut` parameter, and the call says `mut` too
# (E0022 otherwise). `xs[i] = v` changes one element in place, bounds-checked.

struct Point:
    x: int
    y: int

fn shift(mut p: Point, dx: int):
    p.x += dx

fn fill(mut xs: [int], v: int):
    let mut i = 0
    while i < xs.length():
        xs[i] = v
        i = i + 1

fn main() -> int:
    let a = Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
    let mut b = a
    b.x = 10
    print("a.x = " + a.x.to_string() + ", b.x = " + b.x.to_string())

    let mut p = Point { x: 0, y: 0 }
    shift(mut p, 5)
    print("after shift: p.x = " + p.x.to_string())

    let mut xs = [1, 2, 3]
    let ys = xs
    fill(mut xs, 7)
    print("xs[0] = " + xs[0].to_string() + ", ys[0] = " + ys[0].to_string())
    return 0

# 12_closures.astra — closures that capture their surroundings
#
# A closure is written |params| { body } and bound with `let`. It copies the
# variables it uses when it is created, so changing them later does not
# change the closure. Closures are called by name; passing them to other
# functions as values is not supported yet.

fn main() -> int:
    let rate_percent = 8
    let tax = |cents: int| { cents * rate_percent / 100 }
    print("tax on 2500 cents: ${tax(2500)}")

    let greeting = "Hello"
    let greet = |name: str| { greeting + ", " + name + "!" }
    print(greet("Ada"))
    print(greet("Grace"))

    let offset = 10
    let shifted = |x: int| { x + offset }
    offset = 1000
    print("shifted(1) = ${shifted(1)}, offset is now ${offset}")
    return 0

A state machine with enums

# 15_order_workflow.astra — a state machine with enums
#
# Each state is an enum variant that carries its data. `next` handles every
# (state, event) pair: leave one out and the compiler stops with E0021, so a
# new state can't be forgotten. Illegal moves return an error, not a crash.

enum Order:
    Placed(int)
    Paid(int)
    Shipped(str)
    Cancelled(str)

enum Event:
    Pay
    Ship
    Cancel

fn describe(o: Order) -> str:
    match o:
        Order::Placed(id) => return "placed (order ${id})"
        Order::Paid(id) => return "paid (order ${id})"
        Order::Shipped(tracking) => return "shipped, tracking ${tracking}"
        Order::Cancelled(reason) => return "cancelled: ${reason}"

fn next(o: Order, e: Event) -> Result<Order, str>:
    match o:
        Order::Placed(id) =>
            match e:
                Event::Pay => return Result::Ok(Order::Paid(id))
                Event::Cancel => return Result::Ok(Order::Cancelled("customer cancelled"))
                Event::Ship => return Result::Err("can't ship order ${id}: not paid")
        Order::Paid(id) =>
            match e:
                Event::Ship => return Result::Ok(Order::Shipped("TRK-${id}"))
                Event::Cancel => return Result::Ok(Order::Cancelled("refunded"))
                Event::Pay => return Result::Err("order ${id} is already paid")
        Order::Shipped(t) => return Result::Err("${t} has shipped; nothing can change")
        Order::Cancelled(r) => return Result::Err("order is cancelled (${r})")

fn run(name: str, events: [Event]):
    print("${name}:")
    let order = Order::Placed(42)
    print("  ${describe(order)}")
    for e in events:
        match next(order, e):
            Result::Ok(o) =>
                order = o
                print("  -> ${describe(order)}")
            Result::Err(why) => print("  !! ${why}")

fn main() -> int:
    run("happy path", [Event::Pay, Event::Ship])
    run("ship too early", [Event::Ship, Event::Pay, Event::Ship, Event::Cancel])
    run("cancel", [Event::Cancel, Event::Pay])
    return 0

# 19_word_count.astra — a command-line tool that reads standard input
#
#   printf 'the quick brown fox\njumps over the lazy dog\n' | astra run 19_word_count.astra
#
# read_line() returns Some(line) until the input ends, then None. The
# compiler records that this program does I/O: build it with `--deny io` and
# it refuses with E0014, naming the call. A function marked @pure may not do
# any I/O at all.

@pure
fn count_words(line: str) -> int:
    let n = 0
    for w in line.split(" "):
        if w.length() > 0:
            n += 1
    return n

fn main() -> int:
    let lines = 0
    let words = 0
    let chars = 0
    let longest = ""
    let reading = true
    while reading:
        match read_line():
            Some(line) =>
                lines += 1
                words += count_words(line)
                chars += line.length()
                for w in line.split(" "):
                    if w.length() > longest.length():
                        longest = w
            None => reading = false
    print("${lines} lines, ${words} words, ${chars} characters")
    print("longest word: ${longest}")
    return 0

title: Counting by key, then ranking
source:
# 21_maps_and_sorting.astra — counting by key, then ranking
#
# A Map<K, V> holds values by key (int or str keys), remembers insertion
# order, and is a value like a list: `let b = a` copies it. Lists sort in
# place with `sort()` or `sort_by_key(|x| { key })`; the sort is stable, so
# equal keys keep their order.

struct Player:
    name: str
    points: int

fn main() -> int:
    let text = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog the end"
    let counts: Map<str, int> = {}
    for w in text.split():
        if w in counts:
            counts[w] += 1
        else:
            counts[w] = 1
    print("${counts.length()} distinct words, 'the' x${counts["the"]}")

    let words = counts.keys()
    words.sort_by_key(|w| { -counts[w] })
    print("most common: ${words[0]}, then ${words[1]}")

    match counts.get("cat"):
        Some(n) => print("cat x${n}")
        None => print("no cat")

    let scores = [41, 7, 99, 7, 63]
    scores.sort()
    print("lowest ${scores[0]}, highest ${scores[scores.length() - 1]}")
    scores.reverse()
    print("first after reverse: ${scores[0]}")

    let players = [Player { name: "Ada", points: 30 }, Player { name: "Lin", points: 45 }, Player { name: "Bo", points: 30 }]
    players.sort_by_key(|p| { -p.points })
    for p in players:
        print("${p.name} ${p.points}")
    return 0

title: Records, a stack with its own methods, and loops
source:
# 22_warehouse_ledger.astra — records, a stack with its own methods, and loops
#
# Two structs may share field names: a literal is the struct it names, and
# its fields can come in any order. A struct can define its own `push` and
# `to_string`. A range is evaluated once, so a loop may grow the list it
# walks, and `xs[f()] += v` calls f() once.

struct Stock:
    sku: str
    qty: int

struct Order:
    sku: str
    qty: int

impl Stock:
    fn label(self) -> str:
        return "${self.sku}: ${self.qty} in stock"

impl Order:
    fn label(self) -> str:
        return "${self.sku}: ${self.qty} ordered"

struct Undo:
    steps: [str]

impl Undo:
    fn push(mut self, step: str):
        self.steps.push(step)
    fn to_string(self) -> str:
        return "Undo(${self.steps.length()} steps)"

fn slot(sku: str) -> int:
    print("  looking up ${sku}")
    if sku == "bolt":
        return 0
    return 1

fn main() -> int:
    let shelf = [Stock { qty: 40, sku: "bolt" }, Stock { sku: "nut", qty: 15 }]
    let order = Order { qty: 12, sku: "bolt" }
    print(shelf[0].label())
    print(order.label())

    let log = Undo { steps: [] }
    shelf[slot(order.sku)].qty -= order.qty
    log.push("ship ${order.qty} ${order.sku}")
    print(shelf[0].label())

    # Restock every item that is low; restocking adds a line to the plan
    # while the loop runs, and the loop still visits only the original items.
    let plan = ["check bolt", "check nut"]
    for i in 0..plan.length():
        if shelf[i].qty < 20:
            plan.push("restock ${shelf[i].sku}")
            log.push("restock ${shelf[i].sku}")
    for p in plan:
        print(p)
    print(log.to_string())
    return 0
